To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) both monkeys and rats tolerated more electric shock when the interval between increments of the aversive stimulus was short, and (2) monkeys tolerated more shock when the size of the increment was small, and when the size of both the incremental and decremental steps were small.

(1) monkeys will tolerate more shock if the interval between incremental increases in shock amplitude is shorter than if it is longer, and (2) monkeys will tolerate a larger increment in shock amplitude if the decremental step is smaller than if it is larger, or if both the incremental and decremental steps are smaller than if they are larger.
The greater the frequency of increments in the intensity of electric shock, the greater the amount of shock that monkeys can tolerate without responding.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theory of aversive control.
the effects of the temporal and quantitative parameters of a titration avoidance schedule on the aversive threshold.
the effects of the various parameters of avoidance schedules on avoidance performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the amount of shock a subject will tolerate in a titration schedule depends on a complex interaction among the size of the incremental and decremental steps, the interval between the steps, and the amount of avoidance that is elicited.
, in general, the greater the number of shocks the subject is required to tolerate before he can escape, the greater the amount of shock he will tolerate.
the aversive thresholds obtained in the titration schedule were a function of the amount of avoidance elicited by the procedure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the titration schedule is an excellent method for obtaining aversive thresholds and that these thresholds can be influenced by the parameters of the procedure.

the aversive threshold obtained by a titrating procedure is a function of (1) the amount of avoidance elicited, (2) the size of the increments in aversive stimulation, and (3) the interval between increments.
the titration schedule is an efficient and sensitive method for studying aversive thresholds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a titration schedule can be used as a sensitive measure of the effects of variables on aversive thresholds, and it is a schedule that may be useful in the study of aversive control in general.
the aversive threshold can be increased in monkeys by decreasing the amount of shock required to terminate an avoidance response.

a titration procedure is an effective way of obtaining a threshold for the shock intensity at which a subject will respond, and that the titration procedure is not affected by the presence of a decremental step. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2018 APA, all rights reserved)
